A closure keeps the variable, not its value
as a function bundled together with references to its surrounding state, the

. Each time a scope runs, whether it's a function call, a block or a loop iteration, JavaScript creates an environment that holds that scope's variables. A function created inside keeps a reference to that environment. When the function runs, it looks up each variable there and reads whatever the variable holds at that moment.
Closures from the same scope share their variables
Two functions created in the same call see the same variables. If closures held copies,
MDN's closures guide builds a counter the same way, with three functions that share a single lexical environment. It's also how closures emulate private state: nothing outside can reach
